title: Ecologically valid visual exploration in early neurological rehabilitation: Evaluation of a large-scale (extrapersonal) digital screen test variant of the object-based desk test.
summary: Many stroke patients have trouble searching and exploring their surroundings. This happens because of visual field defects, visuospatial neglect (problems in directing attention to one side of space/body), or both. In order to develop and optimize effective treatments, accurate and reliable ways to measure these problems are needed (see also Grattan & Woodbury, 2017). Today, in clinical routine therapists usually use standard A4 paper-and-pencil tests. In these tests, patients must cross out symbols, bisect lines, or copy drawings. These tests are popular because they are well-tested and easy to use in early neurological rehabilitation. However, the test materials (like lines and numbers) are often abstract. In addition, these paper-and-pencil tests can only measure exploratory behavior within a limited part of the patient’s near space. They cannot measure exploratory behavior that requires eye, head, and body movements to search areas further away or the entire room. However, exploratory behavior in near and far space may differ. For everyday clinical routine, a more comprehensive diagnostic approach is needed to better tailor individualized therapy to specific deficits and to improve prognostic assessments. Thus, in addition to traditional standard tests, there is a need for new, easy-to-use tools in early neurological rehabilitation that objectively and sensitively measure exploratory deficits across a broad spectrum of clinical symptoms and severity levels.
conditions: Patients after stroke with and without visual field defect and/or visualspatial neglect

interventions.name: Patients after stroke with deficits in visual exploration: Visual field defect and/or visuospatial neglect
Patients after stroke without deficits in visual exploration: Without visual field defect and/or visuospatial neglect

Control group without stroke-related brain damage:
CIP/CIM, COPD, cardiac diseases without hypoxic brain damage, thoracolumbar spinal cord injury

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
-able to sit and capable of being tested on the screen in the examination room (no bedside testing)
-suffient language comprehension: Patients must demonstrate a sufficient understanding of instructions
-consent provided by the patient or a legal representative/caregiver
Exclusion criteria:
- gaze palsy, apraxia
- severe aphasic (severe to very severe receptive aphasia), cognitive, or psychiatric disorders that would have complicated or hindered adequate performance of the tests (understanding of tasks), such as in the case of severe frontal lesions
-post-resuscitation patients
